title: Can Your Electric Vehicle Catch Fire During a Hurricane?
subtitle: E.V. batteries that are submerged in saltwater can catch fire after the floods subside, but experts say it’s a rarity.
author: Austyn Gaffney & Brad Plumer

annotations.comment: The article has numerous AI markers like the use of pairs when describing things e.g. "safely and efficiently". It also has various other phrases that I recognise from different AI text that I've worked with before.

The use of several lists suggests AI writing. E.g. "engineers, scientists, and firefighters."
Also, the words "critical" and "key" are commonly used by AI.
This was a tough one. But I'm going to say human-generated, based on the fact that AI doesn't tend to use filler words like 'very' and 'even'. It also uses contractions and ends on a quote.

I am confident this article is AI-generated. The article contains a lot of the common vocabulary (significant, understanding, represents, efficiently, etc.)  and sentence patterns that I see with AI, such as "The car should be inspected by a qualified professional who can safely disconnect the battery and assess any damage." and "With the proper precautions—such as moving your vehicle to safer ground before a storm and seeking professional help if it’s flooded—most risks can be minimized." It's formal, contains some sentimental tone to try and quickly summarize a sense of hope in the topic even though it's not needed, and moreover, the quotes aren't realistic to how most people would speak day-to-day.

The rah-rah conclusion: not to worry folks, the clean, sustainable transportation system is still safe. AI forgot to add "for future generations".
The excessively dramatic introductory sentence.
